pages.text: Why a line? Divide both sides of `pV^n = C` by `V^n`, and `p = C V^(−n)`. Take the log of both sides. The product law from lesson 5 splits the log of `C` times `V^(−n)` into `log C + log V^(−n)`, and the power law brings the `−n` down in front of `log V`. Now put `log p` up the side and `log V` along the bottom, and it is `y = mx + c` from Straight-line graphs. The power has become the gradient, `−n`, and `log C` the intercept.

pages.task: Which line is the straight-line form of `pV^n = C`?
pages.why: Divide by `V^n` to get `p = C V^(−n)`, then take the log of both sides. The product law gives `log C + log V^(−n)`, and the power law turns `log V^(−n)` into `−n log V`. Only `V` carries the power, so only `log V` gets the `n`, and the log is taken of `p` as well as of the right side.

pages.task: Which plot of the capacitor's readings will come out straight?
pages.why: The gap is a plain exponential, `10 − v = 10 e^(−t/47)`. Take ln of both sides: the product law gives `ln(10 − v) = ln 10 + ln e^(−t/47)`, and ln of e to a power is the power, so `ln(10 − v) = ln 10 − t/47`, a straight line against plain `t`. `v` itself is a difference, and no log law splits the log of a difference, so `ln v` stays bent. And `t` sits in the power, not under one, so logging `t` bends the line again.

pages.text: A light meter reads 400, 98, 45, 25 and 16 lux at 1 to 5 m from a small lamp. Logging only the y‑axis leaves a bend; log both and the dots line up, so it is a power law. The gradient, about −2, is the power, so `E = a d^(−2)`, and `a` converts back to about 400 lux. The 98 and 45 lux readings were moved a little, as real readings scatter, so the line goes between them.

pages.name: Which law?
pages.task: These readings lie on a straight line with only the y‑axis logged. Which law do they follow?
pages.why: Logging only `y` gives `log y = log a + x log b` for `y = ab^x`: the unknown sits in the power, so `x` stays on an ordinary axis. `y = ax^n` needs both axes logged, because `x` is raised to a power. And `y = mx + c` is straight before any switch; logging `y` would bend it. The gradient is `log b`, so it converts back like an intercept: here `log b ≈ 0.301`, so `b = 10^0.301 ≈ 2`, and each step of 1 in `x` doubles `y`.

pages.task: Another gas's `log p` against `log V` line passes through (0.2, 1.30) and (0.8, 0.46). What is `n`?
pages.why: The gradient is the fall over the run, `(0.46 − 1.30) ÷ (0.8 − 0.2) = −0.84 ÷ 0.6 = −1.4`. The line is `log p = log C − n log V`, so the gradient is `−n` and `n = 1.4`: a falling line means a positive `n`. Had it come out as 1, the law would be `pV = C`, which for an ideal gas is the isothermal case.

pages.task: The lamp's line misses the 98 lux reading a little. What now?
pages.why: Real readings scatter, so a best-fit line has readings on both sides of it: here 98 lux sits a little below and 45 lux a little above. Moving a handle to chase one reading tips the line off the others. And a wrong law would bend the whole set, as the y-only switch did, not leave one reading a little off.
